Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

vignette: Mazen, a 41‑year‑old Iraqi dancer, had grown up in a small town near Mosul, where the rhythms of daily life were punctuated by the clatter of markets and the cadence of call‑to‑prayer. In 2015, while returning from a family gathering, he was caught in an artillery barrage that turned the quiet evening into a cacophony of exploding shells. The roar of the blasts, the acrid sting of burning plastic, and the sight of shattered glass filled his senses. He was fortunate to escape with only minor injuries, but the memory of the sudden, unblinking violence lodged itself deep in his mind, and the world that followed was forever altered. For months after the attack, ordinary sounds began to mirror that night. In the quiet of his apartment, a distant siren or the distant clatter of construction work could trigger the same wave of terror that the artillery had unleashed. The scent of fresh earth, the damp smell that followed heavy rain, or the metallic tang of soil on the street after a storm would transport him back to that chaotic moment. Even the simple utterance of names—his best friend’s name, “Ali,” or the affectionate nickname “Bint Al-Allah” that his grandmother used—would cut him sharply, as if the voices had carried the weight of the battlefield within them. Each of these triggers set in motion a flurry of negative thoughts and feelings that felt inevitable and inescapable. When the sound of distant artillery rumbled through the air, he felt a sudden wave of numbness flood his chest, as though a deadness had seeped into every cell of his body. The same trigger would make his faith in people and in a higher power crumble: he would think, “I can’t trust anyone to keep me safe anymore,” and the idea that a guardian spirit existed seemed nothing more than an illusion. The realization that he had become a living reminder of war—so fragile that anyone could see the ghost of that night in his eyes—made him feel exposed. He feared that in any conversation or dance step, people could read the story of his terror through his expressions. He had come to believe that his past had carved a permanent scar into his identity, and that the world now viewed him through the same lens of horror he could no longer escape. These intertwined triggers and appraisals tightened like a noose around his daily life. At the dance studio where he rehearsed under the bright lights, the echoing beat of the drum or the echo of his own steps on the wooden floor became uncanny echoes of artillery shells. Each rehearsal felt like a battlefield, each spotlight a flash of gunfire. The scent of the freshly sanded floor, mingling with the outdoor air that seeped through cracked windows, carried the smell of damp earth that was a constant reminder of the day he’d seen his friend collapse on a pile of broken glass. When a fellow dancer called out his name, the memory surged, and his face would flush with a sudden, unbidden dread. These moments accumulated, eroding his confidence in both the art that had once given him purpose and in the people he had trusted to support him. Mazen’s marriage to his wife, Laila, had become strained as his inner world grew more alien to the one he had shared with her. In moments when she spoke of her day or suggested a new choreography, his mind would leap back to the battlefield, and he would withdraw, shutting out the warmth that had once felt so natural. He began to doubt whether he could ever reconcile the life he had once dreamed of—performing on a stage with an audience—to the reality of a man haunted by a sound that now echoed in every hallway of his home. It was the mounting isolation and the loss of his creative spark that finally led Mazen to seek help. He feared that the memories would never fade, that his dancing would end with a hollow heartbeat, and that his marriage might dissolve under the weight of his own fears. He hoped, however, that with guidance he could learn to see the world again, to feel a life beyond the echo of that night.
